articles.title: Before Weil, The Biggest Collapse In Biglaw History Ended In Criminal Court
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

Today’s news that Weil Gotshal is winding down after 95 years has Biglaw reaching for comparisons — and the obvious one is Dewey & LeBoeuf, whose 2012 implosion remains one of the largest law firm collapses in American history. But Dewey’s downfall didn’t end with a bankruptcy filing: prosecutors went on to charge three of the firm’s top leaders with cooking the books to deceive its lenders and auditors. Who are the three executives who ended up as criminal defendants?

Hint: Two of them shared a first name and were known collectively around the firm as “the Steves.” The third kept the books.

See the answer on the next page.

articles.title: OnlyFans Content Creators Seeking To Leave The Industry Could Be Trapped If They Don’t Pay Taxes
articles.content:
Some people turn to adult content platforms such as OnlyFans to generate income. Recently, a few that have made significant amounts of money went on podcasts to explain the life and finances of an adult content creator. Some did not make wise financial decisions with the money they made, which includes not paying taxes. These bad decisions came back to haunt them later.
For most of these content creators, their shelf life is short. But if they leave the industry with a large tax bill, can tax collectors have a say on how they make their money to pay back taxes?
Some content creators get into tax trouble because they are not paying taxes as they go, in other words paying estimated taxes during the year. Generally, content creators for sites like OnlyFans are treated like independent contractors which means that no taxes are withheld from their earnings. This means they must pay income taxes on their net income after deducting ordinary and necessary business expenses. But they must also pay self-employment taxes on their net income which is 15.3% of their net income up to the first $184,500 of income, combined with any W-2 employee wages they receive. The latter tax catches many business owners and independent contractors by surprise.
Many of these people are very young and have not had to make serious financial decisions while growing up. So they used their money to buy expensive clothes, cars, and houses. So that leaves little to no money to pay taxes.
Those who continue to stream and consistently make money will eventually pay off any delinquent taxes through an installment agreement. Hopefully they will also learn to set aside any future income and pay future estimated taxes so they won’t get a bill next April.
But one day, adult content creators must choose a different career for various reasons. Some will lose subscribers and other revenue sources as time passes. Others will stop voluntarily and seek to return to a regular life.
The fortunate ones may be able to get (or return to) jobs that pay well. But many creators who later seek a “normal life” confront practical barriers: their prior work may not translate easily into most jobs, public stigma can hinder hiring, and regular employment may pay far less than prior earnings. So when large tax liabilities remain, the only realistic way to generate the cash needed to pay back taxes is to go back to streaming.
So how would the IRS look at a former adult content creator who makes far less money working a regular job? Would the IRS be willing to settle the debt for less than they owe after listening to their story?
The IRS generally settles tax debts for less than they owe in several ways. The first is the partial-payment installment agreement (PPIA). A PPIA is similar to an income-based repayment plan for federal student loans. The taxpayer will pay a monthly amount based on her income and reasonable living expenses. This payment plan will continue until the tax bill is uncollectible due to the statute of limitations which 10 years unless an exception applies. While this plan can be effective, most taxpayers want relief now rather than wait up to 10 years.
The second way is through an Offer in Compromise Doubt As To Liability. This is where you show the IRS that the tax is incorrect. For adult content creators, maybe the tax is incorrect because the tax returns were prepared incorrectly. This may be a solution where a content creator’s manager handled her financial affairs, including preparing and filing tax returns.
The third way to settle a tax debt is by submitting an Offer in Compromise Doubt as to Collectibility. This basically shows the IRS that it is better off settling the tax debt under alternative terms if they believe that a prolonged conventional installment agreement with the taxpayer will nor result in the collection. To be considered for this option, the taxpayer must disclose all financials, including assets, income, and reasonable living expenses. If the taxpayer makes a large amount of money, has significant assets, or both, the IRS will generally deny an Offer in Compromise.
Finally, the IRS allows the taxpayer to submit an Offer in Compromise Effective Tax Administration if the taxpayer has the resources to pay the tax debt in full but has identified special circumstances. According to the Internal Revenue Manual, the IRS may compromise to promote effective tax administration where compelling public policy or equity considerations identified by the taxpayer provide a sufficient basis for compromising the liability, and there are no other grounds for settling the tax debt.
Can a former adult content creator settle her tax debt through an Offer in Compromise Effective Tax Administration? Can she successfully argue that forcing her to return to streaming adult content to pay taxes is a violation of public policy or is an affront to public morals?
The federal tax laws and the IRS’s operating procedures do not force taxpayers to get a certain job that will most effectively pay an outstanding tax debt Taxpayers remain free to accept lower-paying work and the IRS adjusts installment agreements or evaluates collection potential according to actual income and allowable expenses.
The Treasury Regulations give examples as to when settling a tax debt due to public policy may be considered. But generally, they involve cases where the taxpayers are senior citizens with fixed income and no assets, and people will serious health problems requiring expensive medical care. They also do not list occupations (or former occupations) that deserve special scrutiny or special treatment. The IRS is not authorized to act as an arbiter of the social acceptability of legal income sources.
Adult content creators who experienced sudden high earnings but failed to plan for taxes may not get special treatment or much sympathy because they left the streaming industry. They can use existing settlement programs that can address inability to pay or genuine living-expense hardship. The public-policy/equity branch of the Offer in Compromise Effective Tax Administration remains tightly constrained and is not a vehicle for moral judgments about OnlyFans work or for preferential treatment.
Steven Chung is a tax attorney in Los Angeles, California. He helps people with basic tax planning and resolve tax disputes. He is also sympathetic to people with large student loans. He can be reached via email

articles.title: Elon Musk Says He Saved People From Being Killed By Starlink Through Killing Different People With Starlink
articles.content:
In the Antarctic, in the middle of the ocean, or in one of earth’s several active war zones, if you have internet service, it’s probably through Starlink. Having launched more than 10,000 Starlink satellites into orbit using his rocket company SpaceX, Elon Musk unilaterally controls internet access in the world’s most dangerous and remote places.
Homo sapiens are a communicative species, and also a power-hungry species. Thus, it seems obvious that it is a bad idea to put an entire communications medium in the hands of one man.
It seems especially risky to put an entire communications medium in the hands of the richest man in the history of the world who grows ever increasingly erratic and unhinged. Musk is not well.
Yet, here we are. Close to five years ago, Ukraine was invaded by its neighbor Russia for no reason beyond the fact that Russia wanted to seize Ukrainian land and people. In fighting throughout Ukraine to repel the Russian aggressors, innovative Ukrainian defensive techniques relied on Starlink internet services (sometimes separately branded as Starshield in military contexts) to defeat Russian missiles, drones, and air power.
Meanwhile, Musk has spent hundreds of millions of dollars to become, by far, the biggest donor to Republican candidates this election cycle. He additionally spent hundreds of millions in previous election cycles to elect Trump and other Republicans. It is not unclear which side of America’s political divide Musk is on.
Donald Trump is a doddering old man who does not have any logically consistent policy positions. Any cogent American leader would vigorously support Ukraine.
So, naturally, Trump bounces back and forth on alternatively supporting Ukraine or Russia like a strongly whacked billiard ball. Most recently, Trump yet again turned on Ukraine, and when the Starlink internet access Ukraine relies on to defend its civilians was then mysteriously throttled, Trump denied responsibility.
After several days of blame-shifting and confusion, Musk came out and said:
Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be. Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week.
To be clear, everyone on the American right is an iredeemable liar, and we won’t know for years whether Trump actually ordered Musk to throttle Ukraine’s internet service, or whether Musk decided to do it all on his own. In either case, we do know that Ukrainian defensive drones fell out of the sky when their Starlink internet access was throttled.
Were some Russians working at oil refineries or shipyards or military depots saved when Musk cut off Ukraine’s Starlink internet access? Perhaps. Yet, we know for a fact that Ukrainian civilians, left defenseless, were killed while Starlink was throttled, including children.
Musk should not be allowed to favor the lives of Russian soldiers and grown industrial workers over the lives of Ukrainian civilians (including women and children). Truman nationalized the steel industry. Wilson nationalized the railroads. This is not unprecedented — no single man, no single for-profit industry, should have unimpeachable control over a necessary element of a country’s national defense. Musk should not be able to make these decisions himself.
Musk claimed SpaceX has never allowed anyone to use Starlink to kill people. But, by throttling Ukraine’s Starlink service, he almost certainly caused the deaths of Ukrainian civilians, among them a 1-year-old child.
It’s almost as if we shouldn’t be letting an out-of-touch, likely sociopathic billionaire who has allegedly ingested more drugs than Mick Jagger decide who lives and who dies.
Musk is a liar. Maybe he saved some Russians by throttling Ukraine’s Starlink access, maybe he didn’t, but he certainly disabled the defenses protecting a number of Ukrainians who were then killed. These decisions should not be left up to the whims of one man, let alone a man like Musk who consistently displays an utter disregard for anyone else on this planet other than himself.
There is a reason why Musk has become, for Republicans, the largest political donor in the history of the world this election cycle. He knows Republicans will do nothing to hold him accountable.
Don’t let this man further consolidate his grip on power. If you don’t want to live in a world wholly controlled by Elon Musk, voting in this midterm election is probably your last chance to prevent it.
Jonathan Wolf is a civil litigator and author of Your Debt-Free JD (affiliate link). He has taught legal writing, written for a wide variety of publications, and made it both his business and his pleasure to be financially and scientifically literate. Any views he expresses are probably pure gold, but are nonetheless solely his own and should not be attributed to any organization with which he is affiliated. He wouldn’t want to share the credit anyway. He can be reached at jon_wolf@hotmail.com.

articles.title: Legal Horror Stories To Keep You Up At Night
articles.content:
It’s Halloween week, so we’re turning off the lights and telling scary stories. But twist! These aren’t about ghosts, they’re about the legal industry in 2026. First up: how the Supreme Court let Alabama bring back a congressional map a federal court found intentionally discriminatory, without offering a word of explanation. Then there’s the Justice Department’s plan to let the Attorney General freeze state bar ethics investigations into DOJ lawyers. And no firm is too elite to get burned: Sullivan & Cromwell had to apologize to a bankruptcy judge for AI hallucinations, and Skadden and Kirkland got hit with a $2 million benchslap for hiding evidence.
We also look at what happens when a law firm starts to unravel. Cadwalader’s merger with Hogan Lovells was supposed to stop the bleeding, but it sent even more partners running for the exits. And Freshfields’ global managing partner lived every lawyer’s nightmare when he accidentally sent the firm’s secret AI spinoff plans to the entire firm, along with a bonus insult to some very important clients.
Listen in, then tell us which story scared you most by emailing tips@abovethelaw.com with your pick for the scariest story of the year.
Kathryn Rubino is a Senior Editor at Above the Law, host of The Jabot podcast, and co-host of Thinking Like A Lawyer. AtL tipsters are the best, so please connect with her. Feel free to email her with any tips, questions, or comments and follow her on Twitter @Kathryn1 or Bluesky @Kathryn1 The post Legal Horror Stories To Keep You Up At Night appeared first on Above the Law.
